title: Clustering Analysis
text:
Load Packages and Data
Check and load packages, ensuring they are sourced from and supported by CRAN.

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, scales, knitr,tidymodels,fpc)
df_raw <- read_csv("data/colombia_customers_processed.csv")



Data Processing

We apply log10​ transformation to handle the long-tail distribution of transaction data, compressing outliers and normalizing the scale. This ensures the model captures behavioral trends more effectively without being distorted by extreme values.
To account for scale differences between value and volume, we normalize features to a mean of 0 and SD of 1. This eliminates unit bias, ensuring each metric carries equal weight in the clustering process.


df_for_clustering <- df_raw %>%
  dplyr::select(customer_id, average_transaction_value, total_transaction_volume) %>%
  mutate(
    log_avg_value = log10(average_transaction_value + 1),
    log_total_vol = log10(total_transaction_volume + 1)
  )
cluster_recipe <- recipe(~ log_avg_value + log_total_vol, data = df_for_clustering) %>%
  step_normalize(all_predictors()) %>%
  prep()
df_cleaned <- bake(cluster_recipe, new_data = NULL)
summary(df_cleaned)

Feature Selection
By selecting core transactional metrics, psychological traits (satisfaction, churn), and demographics, while applying log transformations to skewed values, we build a more precise and holistic customer profile. This streamlines model inputs for better performance while enhancing the ability to capture complex behavioral patterns.

df_for_analysis <- df_raw %>% 
  dplyr::select(
    customer_id, 
    total_transaction_volume, 
    average_transaction_value, 
    satisfaction_score, 
    churn_probability, 
    gender, 
    income_bracket
  ) %>% 
  mutate(
    log_total_vol = log10(total_transaction_volume + 1),
    log_avg_value = log10(average_transaction_value + 1)
  )



Data Validation & Cleaning

# ensure no missing values

Representative Sampling
By setting a random seed and sampling 5,000 records, we significantly enhance computational efficiency while maintaining data representativeness. This reduces processing time for visualization and modeling while ensuring that the analysis remains consistent and reproducible across different runs.

set.seed(123) 
df_sampled <- df_for_analysis %>%
  sample_n(5000) 



Elbow Plot
We iteratively evaluate k values from 1 to 10 and visualize the “Total Within-cluster Sum of Squares” through an Elbow Plot. This helps balance model complexity and precision, allowing us to mathematically identify the “elbow point” where improvements level off, ensuring we select the most meaningful number of clusters.

set.seed(123)
kclusts <- tibble(k = 1:10) %>%
  mutate(
    kmean = map(k, ~kmeans(df_cleaned, .x, nstart = 20)),
    glanced = map(kmean, glance)
  ) %>%
  unnest(glanced)

ggplot(kclusts, aes(k, tot.withinss)) +
  geom_line(size = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Elbow Plot for K-means",
       x = "Number of Clusters (k)",

get_top_n_labels <- function(v, n = 3) {
  v <- na.omit(v)
  if (length(v) == 0) return("None")
  total_count <- length(v)
  top_n <- as.data.frame(table(v)) %>%
    rename(Occupation = v) %>%

title: Clustering Analysis
text:
Load Packages and Data

We begin by initializing the analytical environment with the tidyverse and poLCA ecosystems, ensuring a robust framework for data manipulation and latent class modeling.


pacman::p_load(tidyverse, poLCA, scales, patchwork, lubridate, knitr, dplyr)
df_raw <- read_csv("data/colombia_customers_processed.csv")



Latent Class Analysis (LCA)

Feature selection is focused on two dimensions: demographic traits (e.g., income, occupation) and behavioral indicators (e.g., churn probability, satisfaction) to build a holistic segmentation framework.


df_sampled <- df_raw %>%
  dplyr::select(
    gender, income_bracket, occupation, age_group,        
    total_transaction_volume, churn_probability, satisfaction_score 
  )



Data Validation & Cleaning

To maintain the integrity of our statistical inferences, we perform a rigorous quality check to ensure the dataset is free of missing values before proceeding to model estimation.


# ensure no missing values
print(sapply(df_sampled, function(x) sum(is.na(x))))

                  gender           income_bracket               occupation 
                       0                        0                        0 
               age_group total_transaction_volume        churn_probability 
                       0                        0                        0 
      satisfaction_score 
                       0 




Representative Sampling

A random sample of 5,000 observations is extracted to achieve an optimal balance between computational efficiency and the statistical power required for representative results.


set.seed(123) 
df_sampled <- df_sampled %>% sample_n(5000)



Binning & Factorization

As LCA requires categorical inputs, continuous variables like transaction volume are discretized into ranked tiers, transforming raw metrics into meaningful behavioral levels.


df_sampled <- df_sampled %>%
  mutate(
    vol_level = ntile(total_transaction_volume, 3), 
    churn_level = ntile(churn_probability, 3),
    sat_level = case_when(
      satisfaction_score <= 4 ~ 1,
      satisfaction_score <= 7 ~ 2,
      TRUE ~ 3
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(-total_transaction_volume, -churn_probability, -satisfaction_score)
df_lca_final <- df_sampled %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), factor)) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), as.integer))



Determining Optimal K - BIC Plot

Model selection is guided by the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC). We iterate through multiple cluster counts to identify the “elbow” where model fit and parsimony are perfectly balanced.


f <- as.formula("cbind(gender, income_bracket, occupation, age_group, vol_level, churn_level, sat_level) ~ 1")

bic_list <- c()
for(i in 2:5){
  res <- poLCA(f, df_lca_final, nclass=i, nrep=2, maxiter=2000, verbose=FALSE)
  bic_list[i] <- res$bic
}
plot(2:5, bic_list[2:5], type="b", pch=19, col="#2E86C1", 
     main="Model Selection: BIC Plot", xlab="Number of Clusters", ylab="BIC Score")










Final Model Execution

With the optimal K identified, we execute the final model to assign each customer to their most probable latent class, providing the basis for our segment profiles.


set.seed(123)
lca_best <- poLCA(f, df_lca_final, nclass=3, nrep=10, maxiter=5000, verbose=FALSE)

df_results <- df_lca_final %>%
  mutate(cluster = as.factor(lca_best$predclass))



Clustering Analysis Dashboard

This visualization translates complex model outputs into actionable insights, mapping the average behavioral signatures of each cluster to define their unique market characteristics.


p1 <- df_results %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(across(c(vol_level, churn_level, sat_level), mean)) %>%
  pivot_longer(-cluster, names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Variable, y = Value, color = cluster, group = cluster)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.8) + 
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(1, 3), breaks = 1:3, labels = c("Low", "Med", "High")) +
  labs(title = "Cluster Behavioral Profiles", 
       subtitle = "Line plots showing the average level of key metrics",
       x = "Behavioral Variable", y = "Average Level") +
  theme_minimal()

Warning: Using `size` aesthetic for lines was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
ℹ Please use `linewidth` instead.

print(p1)









lookup_table <- df_sampled %>%
  mutate(occ_id = as.integer(as.factor(occupation))) %>%
  dplyr::select(occupation, occ_id) %>%
  distinct()

p2_v2 <- df_results %>%

  left_join(lookup_table, by = c("occupation" = "occ_id")) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = cluster, fill = occupation.y)) + 
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Detailed Occupation Mix", 
       subtitle = "Who are these people? (By real job titles)",
       x = "Cluster", y = "Percentage Share", fill = "Job Title") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.text = element_text(size = 8))

print(p2_v2)









get_mode <- function(v) {
  uniqv <- unique(v)
  uniqv[which.max(tabulate(match(v, uniqv)))]
}
persona_summary <- df_results %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(
    Segment_Size = n(),
    Top_Occupation = get_mode(occupation), 
    Top_Age_Group = get_mode(age_group),
    Top_Gender = get_mode(gender),
    Avg_Volume_Level = round(mean(as.integer(vol_level)), 1),
    Avg_Churn_Risk = round(mean(as.integer(churn_level)), 1),
    Avg_Satisfaction = round(mean(as.integer(sat_level)), 1)
  )

print(persona_summary)

Cluster 1: Elite Loyalists (Size: 1,344)

Profile: High-skilled professionals (Engineers, Doctors, Lawyers).
Insight: Despite being high-value, they have the lowest satisfaction (1.16). They are “silent sufferers” who stay out of necessity but are unhappy with the service.




Cluster 2: At-Risk Dissatisfieds (Size: 1,382)

Profile: Service sector workers (Sales, Waiters, Mechanics).
Insight: The most critical group with the highest churn risk (2.86/3.0) and low satisfaction. They are actively looking to leave the bank.

Cluster 3: Stable Casual Users (Size: 2,274)

Profile: Stable middle-class roles (Teachers, Accountants, Architects).
Insight: The most reliable segment. They exhibit the lowest churn risk (1.45) and the highest relative satisfaction, serving as the bank’s stable revenue base.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
3. Distribution of Key Variables
To understand the overall characteristics of the dataset, we first examine the distribution of key behavioral and engagement variables.
Some highly skewed variables, such as transaction volume and transaction counts, are log-transformed using log1p() to reduce skewness and improve visualization clarity.
The variables are then reshaped into long format using pivot_longer() so that multiple histograms can be displayed simultaneously using facet_wrap().

data_cleaned %>%
  mutate(
    log_total_tx_volume = log1p(total_tx_volume),
    log_tx_count = log1p(tx_count),
    log_avg_tx_value = log1p(avg_tx_value)
  ) %>%
  select(
    churn_probability,
    customer_tenure,
    satisfaction_score,
    nps_score,
    support_tickets_count,
    active_products,
    log_total_tx_volume,
    log_tx_count,
    log_avg_tx_value
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "darkseagreen3", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal()








These histograms provide an overview of how key indicators are distributed across the dataset and help identify potential skewness, outliers, and variability among customers.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
4. Correlation Analysis of Churn-Related Variables
To examine the relationships between churn probability and customer behavior indicators, a correlation analysis is performed.
Only numerical variables that are relevant to customer engagement, transaction activity, and satisfaction are selected for the analysis.
Spearman correlation is used because it is more robust to non-normal distributions and outliers compared with Pearson correlation.

corr_df <- data_cleaned %>%
  select(
    churn_probability,
    total_tx_volume,
    tx_count,
    avg_tx_value,
    monthly_transaction_count,
    transaction_frequency,
    avg_daily_transactions,
    customer_tenure,
    satisfaction_score,
    nps_score,
    support_tickets_count,
    resolved_tickets_ratio,
    active_products,
    feature_usage_diversity,
    credit_utilization_ratio
  )

corr_mat <- cor(corr_df, use = "complete.obs", method = "spearman")

corrplot(
  corr_mat,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.cex = 0.7
)








The resulting correlation matrix provides a visual overview of the strength and direction of relationships between variables, helping to identify factors that may be associated with higher churn probability.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
5. Supplementary Check: CLV Segment Profiling
Customers are grouped according to their CLV (Customer Lifetime Value) segment to explore whether customer value tiers exhibit different behavioral patterns.
The summary statistics below calculate the average values of key engagement indicators within each CLV segment.

profile_summary <- data_cleaned %>%

Hyperparameter Tuning and Training of Model

repeatcvControl <- trainControl(
  method = "repeatedcv",
  number = 10,
  repeats = 3,          
  verboseIter = TRUE     
)

n_features <- ncol(df_train) - 1      
my_mtry <- floor(sqrt(n_features))  

rf_model <- train(
  churn_probability ~ .,            
  data = df_train,
  method = "ranger", 
  trControl = repeatcvControl, 
  num.trees = 50,                  
  importance = "impurity", 
  tuneGrid = data.frame(
    mtry = my_mtry, 
    min.node.size = 5,
    splitrule = "variance"
  )
)


df_test$fit_forest <- predict(rf_model, df_test)
test_r2 <- cor(df_test$churn_probability, df_test$fit_forest)^2

  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "darkgreen") +

  labs(x = "Actual Churn Probability", 
       y = "Predicted Churn Probability",
       title = paste0("Test R-squared: ", round(test_r2, digits = 3))) + 
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 8),

        title = element_text(size = 10))
